source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Continue respiratory and neurologic monitoring because opioid toxicity can recur as naloxone wears off.","B":"Stop close monitoring once the client stays awake and speaks normally for a short period.","C":"Do not give additional naloxone if respiratory depression returns after the initial response.","D":"Monitor only for acute withdrawal because recurrent respiratory depression is no longer expected."}}
source_row.rationale: The duration of many opioids can exceed naloxone's duration, so recurrent respiratory or CNS depression may occur after initial improvement. Continued surveillance is required and repeat naloxone may be necessary. Option A is correct; B stops surveillance too early, C contradicts repeat-dosing guidance, and D ignores recurrent toxicity risk.
source_row.source_detail: Repeat Administration/Dosage and Administration: after a satisfactory response, keep the patient under continued surveillance and administer repeated naloxone doses as necessary because the duration of action of some opioids may exceed that of naloxone. Current DailyMed naloxone hydrochloride injection label, cited version 10 and published in 2026; live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: medication administration, adverse effects/interactions, reversal, monitoring and teaching. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
source_row.stem: A client with respiratory depression from a long-acting opioid improves after naloxone. Which nursing action is most important next?
